question: Can a class-balanced LightGBM with validation-tuned, group-specific decision thresholds give a smaller sex-based demographic parity gap in allocation decisions than a standard unconstrained logistic regression on the public Adult dataset, at a small cost in accuracy?
method: Stand-in for multi-agent reward allocation: each person is an agent, income >50K is the reward-worthy outcome, sex is the sensitive attribute. Stratified 75/25 train/test split (seed 42); training part split 80/20 into fit/validation. Baseline: unconstrained logistic regression, single 0.5 threshold. Improved: class-balanced LightGBM with per-sex thresholds chosen on validation to equalise allocation rates. Models run with seeds 42, 43, 44.
metric_name: demographic parity difference on test (|allocation rate F - M|)
baseline: Unconstrained standard logistic regression (one-hot categoricals, standardised numerics), predicted positives at threshold 0.5.
improved: Class-balanced LightGBM (fit on fit split) with separate thresholds for Female and Male chosen on the validation split to minimise the allocation-rate gap (ties broken by validation accuracy).
notes: Single stratified split (seed 42); seeds 42-44 vary only model randomness. No hyperparameter search was run; LightGBM settings are fixed. Thresholds are selected on the validation split, never on test. Both models are trained on the fit split only. Sex is included as a feature in both models. Standard deviations are population std (ddof=0) over 3 seeds; logistic regression is deterministic so its std is 0. Demographic parity ignores base-rate differences and the equal-opportunity gap is reported as a secondary fairness check. Results are from the public Adult data, not the paper's reinforcement-learning setting.
